items.followUp: Why is the ability to produce fertile offspring used to distinguish species of sexually reproducing organisms?

rubric.why: Shows why the usual interbreeding test is unsuitable for unicellular organisms.
rubric.description: Unicellular organisms generally reproduce asexually, so interbreeding does not apply.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they reproduce asexually or do not interbreed.

rubric.why: Identifies a basis used to classify unicellular organisms instead.
rubric.description: They are classified using similarities in their characteristics.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning similarities or shared characteristics.

modelAnswer: The interbreeding criterion is not suitable for most unicellular organisms because they reproduce asexually and do not interbreed.
They are therefore grouped into species by similarities in their characteristics.

items.followUp: State two contributions of Carolus Linnaeus to the classification of organisms.

rubric.why: Binomial nomenclature is a major contribution associated with Linnaeus.
rubric.description: Introduced the system of binomial nomenclature for naming organisms.
rubric.how: Award for naming the system or describing its two-word naming method.

rubric.why: Linnaeus also arranged organisms into broad kingdoms.
rubric.description: Classified organisms into the kingdoms Plantae and Animalia.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the two kingdoms or stating that he classified plants and animals.

modelAnswer: Carolus Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature, in which each organism is given a two-word scientific name.
He classified organisms into two kingdoms: Plantae and Animalia.

items.followUp: Name the four phases of mitosis in their correct order.

rubric.why: These are the four phases of karyokinesis in the correct order.
rubric.description: Names all four phases in order.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for all four correct in order; 1 mark for two or three correct phases or a minor ordering error.

modelAnswer: The four phases of karyokinesis, in order, are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.

items.followUp: What are the main products of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: The reaction converts light energy into chemical energy carriers.
rubric.description: States that light energy is converted into chemical energy, such as ATP and NADPH.
rubric.how: Award for the energy conversion or for naming ATP and NADPH.

rubric.why: Photolysis of water and oxygen release are key events in this reaction.
rubric.description: States that water is split and oxygen is released.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning water splitting and oxygen release.

modelAnswer: The light-dependent reaction is the stage of photosynthesis in which chlorophyll absorbs light energy and converts it into chemical energy in ATP and NADPH.

items.followUp: How does an enzyme-substrate complex form?

rubric.why: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.
rubric.description: The active site binds a specific substrate because their shapes are complementary.
rubric.how: Award for describing substrate binding or specificity of the active site.

rubric.why: Binding enables the enzyme to catalyse the reaction.
rubric.description: The active site positions the substrate for the reaction, forming an enzyme-substrate complex and helping catalyse the reaction.
rubric.how: Award for naming the complex or explaining the catalytic role.

modelAnswer: The active site is the part of an enzyme where a specific substrate binds because their shapes are complementary.
This binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex, allowing the enzyme to catalyse the reaction.

items.followUp: What is the function of veins? Give two points.

rubric.why: The direction of blood flow is the main function of arteries.
rubric.description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to body organs.
rubric.how: Award for stating that blood flows away from the heart.

rubric.why: These are characteristic functions or features that support arterial transport.
rubric.description: Usually carry oxygenated blood and withstand blood pressure with thick, elastic walls.
rubric.how: Award for one correct additional function or characteristic; allow mention that the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.

modelAnswer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body organs.
They usually carry oxygenated blood and have thick, elastic walls to withstand the high pressure of blood flow (the pulmonary artery is an exception).

items.followUp: Explain one way that excessive transpiration can damage a plant.

rubric.why: Excessive transpiration removes more water than the plant can replace.
rubric.description: Excessive transpiration causes too much water to be lost from the plant.
rubric.how: Award for identifying excessive water loss.

rubric.why: Water loss can cause visible damage or reduce plant growth.
rubric.description: The plant may wilt, grow poorly or die; stomatal closure may also reduce photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award for one valid consequence linked to water loss.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is harmful when it is excessive because the plant loses water faster than it can absorb it.
The plant may wilt, its growth may be reduced, and it may eventually die.

items.followUp: Describe the cellular level of organization and give two examples of cell structures.

rubric.why: Molecules are formed from atoms at this level of organization.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that molecules consist of atoms or are formed when atoms combine.

rubric.why: Molecules contribute to the structures that make up cells.
rubric.description: Molecules are the building materials of cell structures and organelles.
rubric.how: Award for linking molecules to cell structures, organelles or cells.

rubric.why: Organic biomolecules are important examples at the molecular level.
rubric.description: Gives examples of organic molecules found in organisms.
rubric.how: Award for suitable examples such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids or nucleic acids.

rubric.why: Inorganic substances are also part of the molecular level.
rubric.description: Identifies examples of inorganic molecules or substances in organisms.
rubric.how: Award for a suitable example such as water, minerals or carbon dioxide.

modelAnswer: At the molecular level, atoms combine to form molecules, which are the building materials of cell structures and organelles.
Molecules in organisms include organic molecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.
Inorganic substances such as water, minerals and carbon dioxide are also present at this level.
